lesson.title: Islands, Continents, and Ancestry: The Evidence of Biogeography
lesson.summary: Biogeography, the study of where species live and have lived, reveals patterns of geographic distribution that only make sense as descent with modification from a shared ancestor followed by geographic separation, evidence Darwin relied on heavily.
lesson.body:
Biogeography is the study of the geographic distribution of species, both living and extinct, and how that distribution relates to evolutionary history. It asks a deceptively simple question: why do particular species live where they live, and not somewhere else that seems just as suitable? The patterns that answer this question turned out to be some of the most persuasive evidence Darwin had for descent with modification, evidence drawn directly from his own observations during the voyage of the Beagle.

The clearest pattern is that closely related species tend to be found near each other geographically, having apparently diversified from a shared ancestor after that ancestor arrived in a particular region. Darwin's finches, observed across the Galapagos Islands, are the textbook case: a group of closely related finch species, each found on the islands, or a subset of them, differing from each other mainly in beak size and shape suited to different available food sources on each island, all more closely related to each other, and to a single mainland South American finch species, than any of them is to superficially similar seed eating or insect eating birds found elsewhere in the world. That pattern, close relatives clustered on neighboring islands, all more closely related to a nearby mainland species than to distant species that fill a similar ecological role, is exactly what is expected if a small founding population colonized the islands once and then diversified in place. It is not what you would expect if each island's species had been independently placed there to perfectly match its local conditions, in which case there would be no particular reason for island species to resemble the nearest mainland species more than they resemble other, more distant species adapted to similar niches.

This same logic extends beyond islands. Australia's marsupials, a whole radiation of pouched mammals filling ecological roles that placental mammals fill on other continents, are far more closely related to each other than to the placental mammals that superficially resemble them elsewhere, and any similarities there, incidentally, are analogous, not homologous, examples of convergent evolution covered a few chapters back. This pattern of regional clusters of related species, most easily explained by shared descent within a region following geographic isolation from other regions, is repeated across continents and island groups worldwide.

Darwin worked out these patterns without knowing the mechanism that explains some of the deepest cases: continental drift. Long after Darwin, the confirmation of plate tectonics showed that continents which are now widely separated, including Australia, South America, Africa, Antarctica, and India, were once joined together in an ancient supercontinent, and that some very old lineages found today only on these now separated landmasses share a common ancestor that lived before the continents split apart, then diversified separately once ocean came to separate their descendants. Plate tectonics did not replace Darwin's biogeographic argument, it extended it, giving a physical mechanism for the oldest and largest scale patterns, while Darwin's original observations about islands and nearby mainlands, driven by ordinary dispersal and geographic isolation rather than continental movement, remain just as valid an argument today as when he made them.
